en: Alas, there is a God to judge your cruelty.
You made them call him another man’s son,
My child left of my khan.
Every day you seared my soul;
By giving me as booty to the enemy,
You burned my soul again and again.
You became my enemy and cast me aside,
But God has freed my hands!
I have come to dig your grave,
I have come to cut off your road!
Now I will bind your fortune,
I will tear your throne away!
I will tear down your roof-ring and level it,
I will turn spring into autumn before its time.
My fury has come; I will lay you flat,
I will hack your life away in pieces,
I will swallow your blood like kumis.
I will end your reign as khan,
I will crush and chew your liver.
You burned me before I could burn;
May you burn and become an ember like me,
Blazing and consumed by fire,
May you vanish as I nearly did.
May you see no daylight, but only night,
May you become charcoal, may you become ash.
You wronged me not once but a thousand times;
Swaggering and strutting,
Why did you stir up so much strife?
From the very beginning, warrior,
Ninety beasts were slaughtered for your feast,
And from the first, mighty Kanchoro,
You were given the name Kanchoro.
You became a brother born of one nest,
But at heart you became an enemy.
You ruined the country and destroyed the people,
You spilled blood and slaughtered the khan.
You plunged the old into misery,
You brought evil upon everyone.
As though the Kyrgyz and Argyn did not exist,
You drove them all away together,
Disdaining them, you put out their hearths.
You increased your levies;
Why did you make them suffer so?
You drowned your fold in blood,
You carried your cruelty beyond all bounds,
You concealed your true malice,
You spread your conflict throughout the land.
Stirring bitter turmoil and strife,
You let the Jediger raid us.
When my uncle Bölökbay was being struck down,
I ran about begging for his life.
I threw myself before the musket,
Pleading, “Dear brother-in-law!”
Heedless of my pleas for life,
You slaughtered all my people.
You raised a hell as high as a mountain;
At the entrance to the treasury,
At the mountain of Kayypchy,
On the slopes of Kan-Jaylak,
You massacred Bölökbay’s men.
The golden-cheeked battle-axe,
Grasping and brandishing it in my hand,
To Kyyaz, son of Bagysh,
You gave it away as booty.
You split my crown and rubbed in salt,
You slit my soles and put worms in them,
Clothed me in a coarse felt cloak,
And mounted me on a dun mare.
This wretched soul once untouched by harsh winds,
Came to yearn even for that felt cloak;
Whatever I touched became embers,
Whatever I ate became filth.
Captured, I sobbed bitterly,
Shrieking as I endured humiliation;
My days of happiness were few,
And wrathful Kyyaz became my foe.
The moonless night was dark;
For fourteen years I was a slave woman,
Gathering firewood and tending livestock.
We collapsed, then struggled upright,
And in that way we vanished.
Wailing and weeping, we were disgraced;
We grew up as orphans.
I shall bring my people down from the hills,
I shall take my revenge without being told.
You stripped off my robe as booty;
Now I shall perform a marvel,
And the quarrel will deepen in the end.
When this sly one runs out of schemes,
They will pitch their camp beside you.
Saying, “We were born as true brothers,”
They will swear oaths to each other.
Growing fat and thriving in secret,
They will gather armor that arrows cannot pierce,
And muster troops from the foremost peoples.
They will steep poison in your churn,
And thus bring about your end.
Your gifts will not be worth a coin
When hardship rises boldly against you.
Your kindness will melt like an ice floe;
Your great wealth will not be worth a scrap of iron.
May the crooked-hearted wretch go mad;
When he grows fat, he will ravage your borders.
All your works will become like charcoal;
When he grows strong, he will ruin your camp.
He will divide your fame down the middle,
And set your village ablaze.
He will turn your wife into an enemy,
At last destroying your honor,
Exhausting the reach of all your designs,
And utterly stripping away your worth.
Yesterday, when an army covering the earth arrived,
Külchoro, were you not there in the fray?
When mortal lives fell thick as flies,
When cunning men broke the ranks,
And many lives were shot away in battle,
When steeds wheeled under charging riders,
When the uproar split the sky,
And heroes met in combat,
From among your own men came
A double-tongued saboteur.
You two Jediger stand side by side;
May this accursed wretch sink into the earth!
This is the very face of treachery,
Broad-tongued and four-square,
This is the very face of deceit.
On the rise beyond the branching pass,
You looked askance across your ridge,
Upon your murderous, turbulent evil—
If only the earth would bear it.
You betrayed us by revealing the secret,
You burned the palace and spread the fire,
You laid waste to all and seized the frontier.
You turned your words toward treason;
Burn to death, you mad wretch!
You stirred up countless feuds and quarrels.
Whenever you wished, in this land—
Where is the blessed night, the night of joy?
Yesterday, when bored, we hunted roe deer;
When not bored, the dear people
Romped and played freely.
Where are the days we had before?
Ruling the people and keeping the nation,
You have become sultan of the Argyn.
Shattering all these people to pieces,
You have sucked them dry like a black leech.
You brought slaughter and seized the frontier,
You destroyed all and lit a fire within,
You sharpened your spear to excess,
You began your wicked frenzy.
Bent old folk and young children
You left without descendants.
You swaggering madman,
Your sin will fall upon yourself,
Your guilt upon your black-crowned head.
Can one prosper by harboring a traitor?
Wild in thought and foul at heart,
Strange in tidings and mighty in venom—
Can Kanchoro truly be a brother?
Would a son of man tend as a brother
A boar that gores from among the herd,
Or call a dragon his kin?
Without taking revenge on that burning wretch,
Dear brother-in-law who made him your guardian,
Can your deed be pleasing to God?
At heart he is our enemy;
In the end, the conflict will multiply,
Son, have you forgotten this?
When they buried you beneath a haystack,
Cut open your shoulder and gouged it,
Enslaved your heroic soul,
And made you gather firewood
For forty hardened herdsmen,
It was Kanchoro who inflicted that disgrace,
And valiant Kyyaz who seized your hands;
It was he who gave the command,
A foe more sinister than any mortal.
Will you not repay the slaughter
And humiliation, Külchoro?
Will you not offer the madman
As a sacrifice, Külchoro?
Let such a traitor disappear,
And let your affairs become clear as glass!
From rocky, cliff-bound Keng-Kol,
We have come to recover our people;
From the pig swollen with wrath,
We have come to take revenge.
From the scattered, ruined Kyrgyz,
We have come to gather counsel;
From the dragon-shaped pig,
We have come to exact vengeance!
The finest among us are our khans;
Drinking red blood and swallowing dust,
Let us all perish together.
Let us snap in a row like threads of hair,
Our precious lives we would not spare.
Let our blood flow like water;
How can our souls find rest
If we swallow grief without revenge?
How can our souls find rest
Without fighting and drinking blood?
The past disgrace and great calamity—
If you are a man, Külchoro,
Take them to heart.
God the Creator made humankind;
If every soul were weak,
All would wander aimlessly.
In the remote tract where no horse could travel,
Upon you and my noble uncle
They drew their bows like pouring rain,
And shot arrows like falling hail.
Stirring total turmoil and strife,
They drove the people into terror,
Seized the land where the nation made its living,
Passed the heights and took the mountain belt.
Desiring wicked turmoil,
Your two uncles Chynkojo and Toltoy—
Claiming, “Those two uncles slaughtered them,”
They incited valiant Kyyaz.
They camped along the Kök-Ötök,
And reveled together with Kyyaz.
Their blood-grooved iron-shafted spears
They gripped short and brandished,
And without sparing a single one of you,
They unleashed a massacre.
They drenched their spears in blood,
And every precious, worthy life
They felled and laid upon the earth.
Blood-red calamity Kanchoro
Planted his steel against the ground,
And never once regarded
The kinship of distant relatives.
With their matchcords glowing red,
Shayymbet and Baytaylak
Destroyed all the khans’ sons,
Those fire-scorched swine.
They pierced them through and took the khans,
And took the lives of those who deemed themselves mighty;
Red gold and blue silver,
And countless herds they seized as plunder.
Climbing a hill, he shouted,
And summoned an army of ten thousand.
In long boots and leather trousers,
With a pacing mare and crimson sheath,
Slave Joydur urged them onward,
Craving ever greater turmoil;
When he spread sorrow far and wide,
It was his own doing.
What manner of man was Kanchoro,
Who fired arrows at his own kin!
The wrathful Chürök began,
And she and Kanykey flared with rage;
With the fluttering life within her breast,
The furious woman launched
A great and dreadful conflict.
That leopardess, your mother Kanykey,
